full_judgment: 9. It is, however, not inconceivable that sometimes situations may arise when for reason beyond the control of the trial judge, the trial of a case cannot be concluded within the specified time. In that case if the above provision of law is strictly applied the offenders are likely to go unpunished resulting in a failure of justice. An argument has, therefore, been made that see him 339C being a procedural law should be construed liberally. It is true that ordinarily procedural laws are not to be given that primary as would defeat the ends of justice. But if a law even though it be procedural in character insists that an act must be done within a particular time providing for certain consequence to follow, if the act is not done the courts are bound to enforce the law as it stands. To take for example, the Limitation Act is generally regarded as procedural in character yet it is to be strictly enforced as section 3 of the Act expressly provides for consequences. 10. It may however be mentioned that the time limit of 120 days as stipulated in sub section (2) has now been extended to hundred and forty days and a provision for revival of cases stopped under sub section (4) has been made under Ordinance No. XXIII of 1986. With the amendment the possibility of there being such an eventuality is now eliminated to a great extent.
